Abstract.

Let ff be a generically finite polynomial map f:ℂn→ℂmf:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{m} of algebraic degree dd. Motivated by the study of the Jacobian Conjecture, we prove that the set SfS_{f} of non-properness of ff is covered by parametric curves of degree at most d−1d-1. This bound is best possible.

Moreover, we prove that if X⊂ℝnX\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is a closed algebraic set covered by parametric curves, and f:X→ℝmf:X\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} is a generically finite polynomial map, then the set SfS_{f} of non-properness of ff is also covered by parametric curves. Moreover, if XX is covered by parametric curves of degree at most d1d_{1}, and the map ff has degree d2d_{2}, then the set SfS_{f} is covered by parametric curves of degree at most 2​d1​d22d_{1}d_{2}.

As an application of this result we show a real version of the Białynicki-Birula theorem: Let GG be a real, non-trivial, connected, unipotent group which acts effectively and polynomially on a connected smooth algebraic variety X⊂ℝnX\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then the set F​i​x​(G)Fix(G) of fixed points has no isolated points.

Key words and phrases: 
affine variety, semialgebraic set, the set of non-properness, parametric curve, degree of a curve

14R25, 14P10, 14R99.

1. Introduction

Let f:X→Yf:X\rightarrow Y be a generically finite polynomial map between affine varieties.

Definition 1.1.

We say that ff is proper at a point y∈Yy\in Y if there exists an open neighborhood UU of yy such that f|f−1​(U):f−1​(U)→Uf|_{f^{-1}(U)}:f^{-1}(U)\rightarrow U is a proper map. The set of points at which ff is not proper is denoted by SfS_{f}.

The set SfS_{f} was first introduced by the first author in [6] (see also [7, 8]). It is a good measure of non-properness of the map ff, and it has interesting applications in pure and applied mathematics [9, 15, 13]. The first author proved the following property of the set SfS_{f} when the base field is ℂ\mathbb{C}.

Theorem 1.2 (Theorem 4.1 [11]).

Let XX be an affine variety over ℂ\mathbb{C}, and let f:X→ℂmf:X\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{m} be a generically finite polynomial map. If XX is ℂ\mathbb{C}-uniruled (covered by polynomially parametric curves), then the set SfS_{f} is also ℂ\mathbb{C}-uniruled.

The first aim of this paper is to give a numerical form of Theorem 1.2. We introduce the notion of degree of uniruledness and we estimate this degree in some cases. In particular if ff is a generically finite polynomial map f:ℂn→ℂmf:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{m} of algebraic degree dd, we prove that the set SfS_{f} of non-properness of the map ff is covered by parametric curves of degree at most d−1d-1. This bound is best possible.

The second aim of our paper is to generalize Theorem 1.2 to the field of real numbers (see Theorem 4.11):


Let XX be a closed algebraic set over ℝ\mathbb{R}, and let f:X→ℝmf:X\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} be a generically finite polynomial map. If XX is ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruled, then the set SfS_{f} is also ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruled.

Our third aim is to prove a real counterpart of the following theorem of Białynicki-Birula.

Theorem 1.3 ([1]).

If a connected, unipotent, algebraic group acts on an irreducible affine algebraic variety X⊂ℂnX\subset\mathbb{C}^{n}, then the set F​i​x​(G)Fix(G) of fixed points of this action has no isolated points.

The proof from [1] is cohomological, and it cannot be extended to the real case. In the last section, as an application of our methods, we modify our approach from [10] and we give a real counterpart of the result of Białynicki-Birula (Corollary 5.3):


Let GG be a real, non-trivial, connected, unipotent group which acts effectively and polynomially on a connected smooth closed algebraic variety X⊂ℝnX\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then the set F​i​x​(G)Fix(G) is ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruled. In particular, it has no isolated points.

2. Preliminaries

Unless stated otherwise, 𝕂\mathbb{K} is an arbitrary algebraically closed field (the real field case is explained in Section 4). All affine varieties are considered to be embedded in an affine space.

The study of uniruled varieties in projective geometry, that is, varieties possessing a covering by rational curves, has a long history. In affine geometry it is more natural to consider polynomially parametric curves (see the definition below) than rational ones. Therefore in [7] (see also [13]) the first author defined 𝕂\mathbb{K}-uniruled varieties as those which are covered by polynomially parametric curves. In [10] we refined this definition for countable fields. In this paper we introduce and study the corresponding quantitative parameter, the degree of 𝕂\mathbb{K}-uniruledness.

Definition 2.1.

An irreducible affine curve Γ⊂𝕂m\Gamma\subset\mathbb{K}^{m} is called a polynomially parametric curve of degree at most dd, if there exists a non-constant polynomial map f:𝕂→Γf:\mathbb{K}\rightarrow\Gamma of degree at most dd (by the degree of f=(f1,…,fm)f=(f_{1},\dots,f_{m}) we mean maxi⁡deg⁡fi\max_{i}\deg f_{i}). A curve is polynomially parametric if it is polynomially parametric of some degree.

We have the following equivalences (see also [10, Proposition 2.4]).

Proposition 2.2.

Let X⊂𝕂mX\subset\mathbb{K}^{m} be an irreducible affine variety of dimension nn, and let dd be a constant. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    for every x∈Xx\in X there exists a polynomially parametric curve lx⊂Xl_{x}\subset X of degree at most dd passing through xx,

  2. (2)

    there exists an open, non-empty subset U⊂XU\subset X such that for every x∈Ux\in U there exists a polynomially parametric curve lx⊂Xl_{x}\subset X of degree at most dd passing through xx,

  3. (3)

    there exists an affine variety WW of dimension dimX−1\dim X-1 and a dominant polynomial map ϕ:𝕂×W∋(t,w)↦ϕ⁡(t,w)∈X\phi:\mathbb{K}\times W\ni(t,w)\mapsto\phi(t,w)\in X such that degt⁡ϕ≤d\deg_{t}\phi\leq d.

Proof.

The implication (1)⇒(2)(1)\Rightarrow(2) is obvious. To prove (2)⇒(1)(2)\Rightarrow(1) suppose that X={x∈𝕂m:f1(x)=0,…,fr(x)=0}X=\{x\in\mathbb{K}^{m}:f_{1}(x)=0,\dots,f_{r}(x)=0\}. For a point a=(a1,…,am)∈𝕂ma=(a_{1},\dots,a_{m})\in\mathbb{K}^{m} and B=(b1,1:…:bd,m)∈ℙMB=(b_{1,1}:\dots:b_{d,m})\in\mathbb{P}^{M}, where M=d​m−1M=dm-1, let

φa,b:𝕂∋t↦(a1+b1,1​t+⋯+b1,dd​td,…,am+bm,1​t+⋯+bm,dd​td)∈𝕂m\varphi_{a,b}:\mathbb{K}\ni t\mapsto(a_{1}+b_{1,1}t+\dots+b_{1,d}^{d}t^{d},\dots,a_{m}+b_{m,1}t+\dots+b_{m,d}^{d}t^{d})\in\mathbb{K}^{m}

be a polynomially parametric curve. Note that for every d​mdm-tuple b=(b1,1,…,bm,d)b=(b_{1,1},\dots,b_{m,d}) we have OPENφa,λ​b​(t)=φa,b​(λ​t))\varphi_{a,\lambda b}(t)=\varphi_{a,b}(\lambda t)) for every λ∈𝕂∗,\lambda\in\mathbb{K}^{*}, hence the image of φa,b\varphi_{a,b} depends only on the class [b]=B∈ℙM[b]=B\in\mathbb{P}^{M} but not on b.b. We will identify φa,b\varphi_{a,b} with the curve φa,b​(𝕂).\varphi_{a,b}(\mathbb{K}).

Consider the following variety and projection:

𝕂m×ℙM⊃V={(a,b)∈𝕂m×ℙM:∀t,ifi​(φa,b​(t))=0}∋(a,b)→a∈𝕂m.\mathbb{K}^{m}\times\mathbb{P}^{M}\supset V=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb{K}^{m}\times\mathbb{P}^{M}:\forall_{t,i}\;f_{i}(\varphi_{a,b}(t))=0\}\ni(a,b)\rightarrow a\in\mathbb{K}^{m}.

Note that fi​(φa,b​(t))=∑kαi,k​(a,b)​tk,f_{i}(\varphi_{a,b}(t))=\sum_{k}\alpha_{i,k}(a,b)t^{k}, hence the equations {fi(φa,b(t))≡0}\{f_{i}(\varphi_{a,b}(t))\equiv 0\} split into finite number of equations αi,k​(a,b)=0,\alpha_{i,k}(a,b)=0, which are homogeneous with respect to b.b.

From the definition, (a,b)∈V(a,b)\in V if and only if the polynomially parametric curve φa,b\varphi_{a,b} is contained in XX. Hence the image of the projection is contained in XX and contains UU, since through every point of UU passes a polynomially parametric curve of degree at most dd. But since the projective space ℙM\mathbb{P}^{M} is complete and VV is closed, we find that the image is closed, and hence it is the whole XX.

Let us prove (2)⇒(3)(2)\Rightarrow(3). For some affine chart Vj=V∩{bj=1}V_{j}=V\cap\{b_{j}=1\} the above map is dominant. We consider the dominant map

Φ:𝕂×Vj∋(t,ϕ)↦ϕ⁡(t)∈X.\Phi:\mathbb{K}\times V_{j}\ni(t,\phi)\mapsto\phi(t)\in X.

After replacing VjV_{j} by some irreducible component Y⊂𝕂mY\subset\mathbb{K}^{m} (dim⁡(Y)=s\dime(Y)=s) the map remains dominant. On an open subset of XX fibers of the map Φ′=Φ|𝕂×Y\Phi^{\prime}=\Phi|_{\mathbb{K}\times Y} are of pure dimension s+1−ns+1-n; let xx be one of such points. From the construction of the set VV we know that the fiber F=Φ′−1​(x)F=\Phi^{\prime-1}(x) does not contain any line of type 𝕂×{y}\mathbb{K}\times\{y\}, so in particular the image F′F^{\prime} of FF under the projection 𝕂×Y→Y\mathbb{K}\times Y\rightarrow Y (which is a constructible subset of YY) has the same dimension. For a general linear subspace L⊂𝕂mL\subset\mathbb{K}^{m} of dimension m+n−s−1m+n-s-1 the set L∩F′L\cap F^{\prime} is 00-dimensional (indeed, F′F^{\prime} contains an open and dense subset of F′¯\overline{F^{\prime}}). Indeed, in this case we have dim 𝕂×R=dimX\mathbb{K}\times R=\dim X and since the fibers of Φ′\Phi^{\prime} have generically dimension 00, the map Φ′\Phi^{\prime} has to be dominant.

To prove the implication (3)⇒(2)(3)\Rightarrow(2) it is enough to notice that for every w∈Ww\in W the map ϕw:𝕂∋t↦ϕ⁡(t,w)∈X\phi_{w}:\mathbb{K}\ni t\mapsto\phi(t,w)\in X is a polynomially parametric curve of degree at most dd or it is constant. The image of ϕ\phi contains an open dense subset, so after excluding the points with infinite preimages (a closed set of codimension at most one) we get an open set UU with required properties. ∎

Definition 2.3.

We say that an affine variety XX has degree of 𝕂\mathbb{K}-uniruledness at most dd if all its irreducible components satisfy the conditions of Proposition 2.2. An affine variety is called 𝕂\mathbb{K}-uniruled if it has some degree of 𝕂\mathbb{K}-uniruledness.

To simplify our statements we say that the empty set has degree of 𝕂\mathbb{K}-uniruledness zero, in particular it is 𝕂\mathbb{K}-uniruled.

Example 2.4.

Let X⊂𝕂nX\subset\mathbb{K}^{n} be a general hypersurface of degree d<n.d<n. It is well-known (see [12, Exercise V.4.4.3, p. 269] that XX is covered by affine lines, therefore its degree of 𝕂\mathbb{K}-uniruledness is one.

For uncountable (algebraically closed) fields there is also another characterization of 𝕂\mathbb{K}-uniruled varieties (see [13, Theorem 3.1]).

Proposition 2.5.

Let 𝕂\mathbb{K} be an uncountable algebraically closed field, and let X⊂𝕂mX\subset\mathbb{K}^{m} be an affine variety. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    XX is 𝕂\mathbb{K}-uniruled,

  2. (2)

    for every x∈Xx\in X there exists a polynomially parametric curve lx⊂Xl_{x}\subset X passing through xx,

  3. (3)

    there exists an open, non-empty subset U⊂XU\subset X such that for every x∈Ux\in U there exists a polynomially parametric curve lx⊂Xl_{x}\subset X passing through xx.

3. The complex field case

In the whole section we assume that the base field is ℂ\mathbb{C}. The condition that a map is not finite at a point yy is equivalent to it being locally non-proper in the topological sense (there is no neighborhood UU of yy such that f−1​(U¯)f^{-1}(\overline{U}) is compact). This characterization gives the following:

Proposition 3.1 ([6]).

Let f:X→Yf:X\rightarrow Y be a generically finite map between affine varieties. Then y∈Sfy\in S_{f} if and only if there exists a sequence (xn)(x_{n}) in XX, such that xn→∞x_{n}\rightarrow\infty and f⁡(xn)→yf(x_{n})\rightarrow y.

In particular, for a polynomial map f:ℂn→ℂnf:\mathbb{C}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{n}, y∈Sfy\in S_{f} if and only if either dimf−1​(y)>0\dim f^{-1}(y)>0, or f−1​(y)={x1,…,xr}f^{-1}(y)=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{r}\} is a finite set, but ∑i=1rμxi​(f)<μ⁡(f)\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_{x_{i}}(f)<\mu(f), where μ\mu denotes multiplicity. In other words, ff is not proper at yy if ff is not a local analytic covering over yy.

Theorem 3.2.

Suppose f:ℂn→ℂmf:\mathbb{C}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{m} is a generically finite polynomial map of degree dd. Then the set SfS_{f} is covered by parametric polynomial curves of degree at most d−1d-1.

Proof.

Let y∈Sfy\in S_{f}; by an affine transformation we can assume that y=O=(0,0,…,0)∈ℂmy=O=(0,0,...,0)\in\mathbb{C}^{m}. For the same reason we can assume that O∉f−1​(Sf)O\not\in f^{-1}(S_{f}). By Proposition 3.1 there exists a sequence of points xk→∞x_{k}\to\infty such that f⁡(xk)→Of(x_{k})\rightarrow O. Let us consider the line Lk​(t)=t​O+(1−t)​xk=(1−t)​xk,t∈ℂL_{k}(t)=tO+(1-t)x_{k}=(1-t)x_{k},\ t\in\mathbb{C}. Set lk​(t)=f⁡(Lk​(t))l_{k}(t)=f(L_{k}(t)). Of course we have deg lk≤dl_{k}\leq d for every k.k. Moreover, we can assume that deg⁡lk>0\deg l_{k}>0, because infinite fibers cover only a nowhere dense subset of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. Each curve lkl_{k} is given by mm polynomials of one variable:

lk​(t)=(∑i=0dai1​(k)​ti,…,∑i=0daim​(k)​ti).l_{k}(t)=(\sum_{i=0}^{d}a^{1}_{i}(k)t^{i},\dots,\sum_{i=0}^{d}a^{m}_{i}(k)t^{i}).

Hence lkl_{k} corresponds to the uniquely determined point

(a01​(k),…,ad1​(k),a02​(k),…,ad2​(k),…,a0m​(k),…,adm​(k))∈ℂN.(a^{1}_{0}(k),\dots,a^{1}_{d}(k);a^{2}_{0}(k),\dots,a^{2}_{d}(k);\ldots;a^{m}_{0}(k),\dots,a^{m}_{d}(k))\in\mathbb{C}^{N}.

Since for each ii, a0i​(k)→0a^{i}_{0}(k)\rightarrow 0 as k→∞k\rightarrow\infty, we can change the parametrization of lkl_{k} by setting t→λk​tt\rightarrow\lambda_{k}t in such a way that ‖lk‖=1\|l_{k}\|=1 for k≫0k\gg 0 (we consider here lkl_{k} as an element of ℂN\mathbb{C}^{N} with Euclidean norm). Now, since the unit sphere is compact, it is easy to see that there exists a subsequence (lkr)(l_{k_{r}}) of (lk)(l_{k}) which converges to a polynomial map l:ℂ→ℂml:\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{m} with l⁡(0)=Ol(0)=O and deg l≤d.l\leq d. Moreover, ll is non-constant, because ‖l‖=1\|l\|=1 and l⁡(0)=O.l(0)=O.     λ=∞\lambda=\infty; then ‖Lk​(λk​t)‖≥(|λk​t|−1)​‖xk‖\|L_{k}(\lambda_{k}t)\|\geq(|\lambda_{k}t|-1)\|x_{k}\|, and hence ‖Lk​(λk​t)‖→∞\|L_{k}(\lambda_{k}t)\|\to\infty for every t≠0t\neq 0.

Now we show that deg⁡l<d.\deg l<d. The idea of the proof is as follows: Note that every curve lkl_{k} passes through the point f⁡(O)f(O), but the curve l=limlkl=\lim\ l_{k} does not. The reason is that if lk​(tk)=f⁡(O)l_{k}(t_{k})=f(O), then limtk=∞.\lim\ t_{k}=\infty. We show that if deg⁡l=d\deg l=d, then we can bound all tkt_{k}, and consequently we get a contradiction.

Let l⁡(t)=(l1​(t),…,lm​(t))l(t)=(l_{1}(t),\dots,l_{m}(t)) and lk​(t)=(l1k​(t),…,lmk​(t))l_{k}(t)=(l_{1}^{k}(t),\dots,l_{m}^{k}(t)). We can assume that the component l1​(t)l_{1}(t) has maximal degree. When we pass to the limit we get l⁡(t0)=al(t_{0})=a, which is a contradiction, since a=f⁡(O)∉Sf.a=f(O)\not\in S_{f}. Hence deg l<d.l<d. ∎

Now let f:ℂn→ℂnf:\mathbb{C}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{n} be a polynomial map with non-vanishing jacobian. The famous Jacobian Conjecture asserts that in this case ff is a diffeomorphism (see e.g. [2, 5]). Despite many efforts the conjecture is still wide open. The main obstruction for its solution is related to the set SfS_{f} of non-properness of the map ff. Van den Dries and McKenna proved in 19901990 that there is no counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture for which the set SfS_{f} is a union of hyperplanes (see [3]). This suggests that we could solve the Jacobian Conjecture if we had some information about the geometry of the set SfS_{f}. On the other hand, it is well-known that we can reduce the algebraic degree of the map ff to degree 33 (see [2, 4]). The price we have to pay for this reduction is that in practice we have to consider all possible dimensions, even if we try to solve the problem for a fixed dimension. Theorem 3.2 gives the following characterization of the set SfS_{f} for generically finite cubic maps f:ℂn→ℂnf:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}.

Corollary 3.3.

Suppose f:ℂn→ℂnf:\mathbb{C}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{n} is a generically finite cubic map. Then the set SfS_{f} is covered by lines and parabolas. Moreover, if ff is quadratic, then SfS_{f} is covered only by lines.

Theorem 3.4.

Let X=ℂ×W⊂ℂ×ℂnX=\mathbb{C}\times W\subset\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}^{n} be an affine cylinder and let f:ℂ×W∋(t,w)→(f1​(t,w),…,fm​(t,w))∈ℂmf:\mathbb{C}\times W\ni(t,w)\rightarrow(f_{1}(t,w),\dots,f_{m}(t,w))\in\mathbb{C}^{m} be a generically finite polynomial map. Assume that degt⁡fi≤d\deg_{t}f_{i}\leq d for every 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. Then the set SfS_{f} has degree of ℂ\mathbb{C}-uniruledness at most dd.

Proof.

Let y∈Sfy\in S_{f}; by an affine transformation we can assume that y=O=(0,0,…,0)∈ℂmy=O=(0,0,...,0)\in\mathbb{C}^{m}. By Proposition 3.1 there exists a sequence (ak,wk)∈ℂ×W(a_{k},w_{k})\in\mathbb{C}\times W such that (ak,wk)→∞(a_{k},w_{k})\to\infty and f⁡(ak,wk)→yf(a_{k},w_{k})\rightarrow y. Let us consider the line Lk​(t)=((1−t)​ak,wk),t∈ℂL_{k}(t)=((1-t)a_{k},w_{k}),\ t\in\mathbb{C}. Set lk​(t)=f⁡(Lk​(t))l_{k}(t)=f(L_{k}(t)). We can assume that deg⁡lk>0\deg l_{k}>0, because infinite fibers cover only nowhere dense subset of XX. Each curve lkl_{k} is given by mm polynomials of one variable:

lk​(t)=(∑i=0dai1​(k)​ti,…,∑i=0daim​(k)​ti).l_{k}(t)=(\sum_{i=0}^{d}a^{1}_{i}(k)t^{i},\dots,\sum_{i=0}^{d}a^{m}_{i}(k)t^{i}).

As before, lkl_{k} corresponds to the single point

(a01​(k),…,ad1​(k),a02​(k),…,ad2​(k),…,a0m​(k),…,adm​(k))∈ℂN.(a^{1}_{0}(k),\dots,a^{1}_{d}(k);a^{2}_{0}(k),\dots,a^{2}_{d}(k);\ldots;a^{m}_{0}(k),\dots,a^{m}_{d}(k))\in\mathbb{C}^{N}.

Since for each ii, a0i​(k)→0a^{i}_{0}(k)\rightarrow 0 as k→∞k\rightarrow\infty we can change the parametrization of lkl_{k} by setting t→λk​tt\rightarrow\lambda_{k}t in such a way that ‖lk‖=1\|l_{k}\|=1 for k≫0k\gg 0 (we consider here lkl_{k} as an element of ℂN\mathbb{C}^{N} with Euclidean norm). Now, since the unit sphere is compact, there exists a subsequence (lkr)(l_{k_{r}}) of (lk)(l_{k}) which is convergent to a polynomial map l:ℂ→ℂml:\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{m} with l⁡(0)=Ol(0)=O. Moreover, ll is non-constant, because ‖l‖=1\|l\|=1 and l⁡(0)=O.l(0)=O. We can also assume that the limit limk→∞λk=λ\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\lambda_{k}=\lambda exists in the compactification of the field ℂ\mathbb{C}. We consider two cases:

  1. (1)

    λ\lambda is finite; then Lk​(λk​t)=((1−λk​t)​ak,wk)→∞L_{k}(\lambda_{k}t)=((1-\lambda_{k}t)a_{k},w_{k})\to\infty for t≠λ−1.t\not=\lambda^{-1}.

  2. (2)

Corollary 3.5.

Let f=(f1,…,fm):ℂn→ℂmf=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}):\mathbb{C}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{m} be a generically finite map with d=​m​i​nj​maxi​degxj​fid=\emph{min}_{j}\max_{i}\deg_{x_{j}}f_{i}. Then the set SfS_{f} has degree of ℂ\mathbb{C}-uniruledness at most dd.

Let us recall (see [11]) that for a generically finite polynomial map f:X→Yf:X\rightarrow Y with XX being ℂ\mathbb{C}-uniruled the set SfS_{f} is also ℂ\mathbb{C}-uniruled. We have the following ’’quantitative‘‘ counterpart of this result:

Theorem 3.6.

Let XX be an affine variety with degree of ℂ\mathbb{C}-uniruledness at most d1d_{1}, and let f:X→ℂmf:X\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{m} be a generically finite map of degree d2d_{2}. Then the set SfS_{f} has degree of ℂ\mathbb{C}-uniruledness at most d1​d2d_{1}d_{2}.

By Definition 2.3 there exists an affine variety WW with dimW=dimX−1\dim W=\dim X-1 and a dominant polynomial map ϕ:ℂ×W→X\phi:\mathbb{C}\times W\rightarrow X of degree at most d1d_{1} in the first coordinate. The equality dimℂ×W=dimX\dim\mathbb{C}\times W=\dim X implies that ϕ\phi is generically finite, hence so is f∘ϕ:ℂ×W→ℂmf\circ\phi:\mathbb{C}\times W\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{m}, which is of degree at most d1​d2d_{1}d_{2} in the first coordinate. By Theorem 3.4, Sf∘ϕS_{f\circ\phi} has degree of ℂ\mathbb{C}-uniruledness at most d1​d2d_{1}d_{2}. We have the inclusion Sf⊂Sf∘ϕS_{f}\subset S_{f\circ\phi}, and from Theorem 1.2 we know that if non-empty, both sets are of pure dimension dimX−1\dim X-1, so each component of SfS_{f} is a component of Sf∘ϕS_{f\circ\phi}. This implies the assertion. ∎

Example 3.7.

Let f:ℂn∋(x1,…,xn)↦(x1,x1​x2,…,x1​xn)∈ℂnf:\mathbb{C}^{n}\ni(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\mapsto(x_{1},x_{1}x_{2},\ldots,x_{1}x_{n})\in\mathbb{C}^{n}. For n>2n>2 let X={x∈ℂn:x1​x2=1}X=\{x\in\mathbb{C}^{n}:x_{1}x_{2}=1\}, and f:X∋(x1,…,xn)↦(x2,…,xn)∈ℂn−1f:X\ni(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\mapsto(x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{C}^{n-1}. The variety XX has degree of ℂ\mathbb{C}-uniruledness 11. Moreover, deg⁡f=1\deg f=1 and Sf={x∈ℂn−1:x1=0}S_{f}=\{x\in\mathbb{C}^{n-1}:x_{1}=0\}. So the set SfS_{f} has degree of ℂ\mathbb{C}-uniruledness 11. This shows that in general Theorems 3.4 and 3.6 cannot be improved.

Remark 3.9.

By the Lefschetz Principle all the results of this section remain true for an arbitrary algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.

4. The real field case

In the whole section we assume that the base field is ℝ\mathbb{R}. Let us recall that by a real polynomially parametric curve of degree at most dd in a semialgebraic set X⊂ℝnX\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} we mean the image of a non-constant real polynomial map f:ℝ→Xf:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow X of degree at most dd. In general a real polynomially parametric curve need not be algebraic, but only semialgebraic. The real counterpart of Proposition 2.2 is the following.

Proposition 4.1.

Let X⊂ℝnX\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a closed semialgebraic set, and let dd be a constant. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    for every x∈Xx\in X there exists a polynomially parametric curve lx⊂Xl_{x}\subset X of degree at most dd passing through xx,

  3. (3)

    for every polynomial map f:X→ℝmf:X\to\mathbb{R}^{m}, and every sequence xk∈Xx_{k}\in X such that f⁡(xk)→a∈ℝmf(x_{k})\rightarrow a\in\mathbb{R}^{m} there exists a semialgebraic curve WW and a generically finite polynomial map ϕ:ℝ×W∋(t,w)↦ϕ⁡(t,w)∈X\phi:\mathbb{R}\times W\ni(t,w)\mapsto\phi(t,w)\in X such that degt⁡ϕ≤d\deg_{t}\phi\leq d, and there exists a sequence yk∈ℝ×Wy_{k}\in\mathbb{R}\times W such that f⁡(ϕ⁡(yk))→af(\phi(y_{k}))\rightarrow a. Moreover, if xk→∞x_{k}\rightarrow\infty, then also ϕ⁡(yk)→∞.\phi(y_{k})\rightarrow\infty.

Proof.

First we prove the implication (2)⇒(1)(2)\Rightarrow(1). Suppose that X={x∈ℝn:f1(x)=0,…,fr(x)=0g1(x)≥0,…,gs(x)≥0}X=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:f_{1}(x)=0,\dots,f_{r}(x)=0\,g_{1}(x)\geq 0,...,g_{s}(x)\geq 0\}. For a=(a1,…,an)∈ℝna=(a_{1},\dots,a_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and b=(b1,1,…,bd,n)∈ℝMb=(b_{1,1},\dots,b_{d,n})\in\mathbb{R}^{M}, where M=d​nM=dn, let

φa,b​(t)=(a1+b1,1​t+⋯+b1,dd​td,…,an+bn,1​t+⋯+bn,dd​td)\varphi_{a,b}(t)=(a_{1}+b_{1,1}t+\dots+b_{1,d}^{d}t^{d},\dots,a_{n}+b_{n,1}t+\dots+b_{n,d}^{d}t^{d})

be a polynomially parametric curve. If there exists a polynomially parametric curve of degree at most dd passing through aa, then after reparametrization we can assume that it is φa,b\varphi_{a,b} for ∑i,jbi,j2=1\sum_{i,j}b_{i,j}^{2}=1. This means that b∈SM​(0,1)b\in S_{M}(0,1), where SMS_{M} denotes the unit sphere in ℝM\mathbb{R}^{M}. Consider the semialgebraic set

V={(a,b)∈ℝn×SM(0,1):∀t,ifi(φa,b(t))=0,∀t,jgj(φa,b(t))≥0}.V=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\times S_{M}(0,1):\forall_{t,i}\;f_{i}(\varphi_{a,b}(t))=0,\forall_{t,j}\;g_{j}(\varphi_{a,b}(t))\geq 0\}.

For any a∈Xa\in X, by the assumption there is a sequence ak→aa_{k}\rightarrow a such that for every kk there is a polynomially parametric curve φak,bk∈V\varphi_{a_{k},b_{k}}\in V. We can assume that ‖ak‖<‖a‖+1\|a_{k}\|<\|a\|+1 for all kk. Now the polynomially parametric curve φa,b⊂X\varphi_{a,b}\subset X of degree at most dd passes through aa.

We prove (1)⇒(3)(1)\Rightarrow(3). Consider the semialgebraic set VV as above. We have the surjective map

Φ:ℝ×V∋(t,φa,b)→φa,b​(t)∈X.\Phi:\mathbb{R}\times V\ni(t,\varphi_{a,b})\rightarrow\varphi_{a,b}(t)\in X.

Let f:X→ℝmf:X\to\mathbb{R}^{m} be a polynomial map, and suppose f⁡(xk)→a∈ℝmf(x_{k})\rightarrow a\in\mathbb{R}^{m} for a sequence xk∈Xx_{k}\in X. Set g=f∘Φg=f\circ\Phi. Finally, to prove (3)⇒(2)(3)\Rightarrow(2) it is enough to take as ff the identity in the third condition. ∎

Definition 4.2.

We say that a closed semialgebraic set XX has degree of ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruledness at most dd if it satisfies the conditions of Proposition 4.1. A closed semialgebraic set is called ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruled if it has some degree of ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruledness.

Example 4.3.

Let X={(x,y)∈ℝ2:x≥0,y≥0}X=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:x\geq 0,y\geq 0\}. It is easy to check that the degree of ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruledness of XX is 22. It has a ruling {(a,t2):a≥0}\{(a,t^{2}):a\geq 0\}.

Let X⊂ℝnX\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a closed semialgebraic set, and let f:X→ℝmf:X\to\mathbb{R}^{m} be a polynomial map. Let X=ℝ×W⊂ℝ×ℝnX=\mathbb{R}\times W\subset\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n} be a closed semialgebraic cylinder and let f:R×W∋(t,w)↦(f1​(t,w),…,fm​(t,w))∈ℝmf:R\times W\ni(t,w)\mapsto(f_{1}(t,w),\dots,f_{m}(t,w))\in\mathbb{R}^{m} be a generically finite polynomial map. Let L=ϕ⁡(ℝ)L=\phi(\mathbb{R}) be a polynomially parametric curve of degree D.D. For the proof it is enough to note that the mapping ℝ×W∋(t,w)↦(ϕ⁡(t),w)∈L×W\mathbb{R}\times W\ni(t,w)\mapsto(\phi(t),w)\in L\times W is proper nad generically-finite. ∎

Corollary 4.7.

Let f=(f1,…,fm):ℝn→ℝmf=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}):\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} be a generically finite polynomial map with d=​m​i​nj​maxi​degxj​fid=\emph{min}_{j}\max_{i}\deg_{x_{j}}f_{i}. Then the set SfS_{f} has degree of ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruledness at most dd.

The proofs of these facts are exactly the same as in the complex case. To prove a real analog of Theorem 3.6 we need some ideas from [10]. Let XX be a smooth complex projective surface, and let D=∑i=1nDiD=\sum_{i=1}^{n}D_{i} be a simple normal crossing divisor on XX (we consider only reduced divisors). Let graph⁡(D)\graph(D) be the graph of DD, with vertices DiD_{i}, and one edge between DiD_{i} and DjD_{j} for each point of intersection of DiD_{i} and DjD_{j}.

Definition 4.8.

We say that DD a simple normal crossing divisor on a smooth surface XX is a tree if graph⁡(D)\graph(D) is a tree (it is connected and acyclic).

The following fact is obvious from graph theory.

Proposition 4.9.

Let XX be a smooth projective surface and D⊂XD\subset X be a divisor which is a tree. If D′,D′′⊂DD^{\prime},D^{\prime\prime}\subset D are connected divisors without common components, then D′D^{\prime} and D′′D^{\prime\prime} have at most one point in common.

Definition 4.10.

Let X⊂ℝnX\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} (X⊂ℙnX\subset\mathbb{P}^{n})be an algebraic variety. Hence we have a natural embedding X⊂ℂnX\subset\mathbb{C}^{n} (X⊂ℙn​(C)X\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}(C)). By the complexification XcX^{c} of the variety XX we mean the Zariski closure of XX in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} (ℙn​(ℂ)\mathbb{P}^{n}(\mathbb{C})).

Theorem 4.11.

Let X⊂ℝnX\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a closed algebraic set with degree of ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruledness at most d1d_{1}, and let f:X→ℝmf:X\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} be a generically finite polynomial map of degree d2d_{2}. Then the set SfS_{f} is also ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruled. Moreover, its degree of ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruledness is at most 2​d1​d22d_{1}d_{2}.

Let a∈Sfa\in S_{f} and let xk∈Xx_{k}\in X be a sequence of points such that f⁡(xk)→af(x_{k})\rightarrow a and xk→∞.x_{k}\to\infty. By Proposition 4.1 there exists a semialgebraic curve W⊂ℝQW\subset\mathbb{R}^{Q} and a generically finite polynomial map ϕ:ℝ×W∋(t,w)→ϕ⁡(t,w)∈X\phi:\mathbb{R}\times W\ni(t,w)\rightarrow\phi(t,w)\in X such that degt⁡ϕ≤d1\deg_{t}\phi\leq d_{1}, and there exists a sequence (yk)⊂ℝ×W(y_{k})\subset\mathbb{R}\times W such that f⁡(ϕ⁡(yk))→af(\phi(y_{k}))\rightarrow a and yk→∞.y_{k}\to\infty. In particular a∈Sf∘ϕ.a\in S_{f\circ\phi}. If we knew that the mapping ϕ\phi is proper, then Sf∘ϕ⊂SfS_{f\circ\phi}\subset S_{f} and we are done by Theorem 4.5. However, in general it is not true. Our idea is to obtain a suitable compactification ϕ′\phi^{\prime} of the map ϕ\phi, and then to derive all information from the fact that Sf∘ϕ′⊂Sf∘ϕS_{f\circ\phi^{\prime}}\subset S_{f\circ\phi} and Sf∘ϕ′⊂Sf.S_{f\circ\phi^{\prime}}\subset S_{f}.

Let Γ⊂ℝQ\Gamma\subset\mathbb{R}^{Q} be the Zariski closure of WW. We can assume that Γ\Gamma is smooth and irreducible. Denote Z:=ℝ×ΓZ:=\mathbb{R}\times\Gamma. We have the induced map ϕ:Z→X\phi:Z\rightarrow X. Lemma 4.12.

Let ψ:ℝ→ℝm\psi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} be a polynomially parametric curve. If there exist polynomially parametric curves ϕi:ℝ→ℝm,i=1,…,n\phi_{i}:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m},\ i=1,...,n, of degree at most dd with ψ⁡(ℝ)⊂⋃i=1nϕi​(ℝ)\psi(\mathbb{R})\subset\bigcup^{n}_{i=1}\phi_{i}(\mathbb{R}), then ψ⁡(ℝ)\psi(\mathbb{R}) has degree of ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruledness at most 2​d2d.

Proof.

Indeed, let ψ⁡(t)=(ψ1​(t),…,ψm​(t))\psi(t)=(\psi_{1}(t),...,\psi_{m}(t)) and let XX denote the Zariski closure of ψ⁡(ℝ).\psi(\mathbb{R}). Consider the field L=ℝ⁡(ψ1,…,ψm)L=\mathbb{R}(\psi_{1},...,\psi_{m}). By the Lüroth Theorem there exists a rational function g⁡(t)∈ℝ⁡(t)g(t)\in\mathbb{R}(t) such that L=ℝ⁡(g⁡(t)).L=\mathbb{R}(g(t)). Corollary 4.13.

Let XX be a closed algebraic set which is ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruled and let f:X→ℝmf:X\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} be a generically finite polynomial map. Then every connected component of the set SfS_{f} is unbounded.

5. An application of the real field case

As an application we give a real counterpart of a theorem of Białynicki-Birula [1].

Theorem 5.1.

Let GG be a real, non-trivial, connected, unipotent group, which acts effectively and polynomially on a closed algebraic ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruled set X⊂ℝnX\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then the set F​i​x​(G)Fix(G) of fixed points of this action, is also ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruled. In particular, it has no isolated points.

Proof.

First of all let us recall that a connected unipotent group has a normal series

0=G0⊂G1⊂⋯⊂Gr=G,0=G_{0}\subset G_{1}\subset\dots\subset G_{r}=G,

where Gi/Gi−1≅Ga=(ℝ,+,0).G_{i}/G_{i-1}\cong G_{a}=(\mathbb{R},+,0). By induction on dim GG we can easily reduce the problem to G=Ga.G=G_{a}. Indeed, assume the conclusion holds for G=Ga.G=G_{a}. Take a unipotent group GG with dim G=nG=n and assume that the conclusion holds in dimension n−1.n-1. There is a normal subgroup Gn−1G_{n-1} of dimension n−1n-1 such that G/Gn−1=Ga.G/G_{n-1}=G_{a}. Moreover, the set R:=F​i​x​(Gn−1)R:=Fix(G_{n-1}) is ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruled by our hypothesis. Consider the induced action of the group Ga=G/Gn−1G_{a}=G/G_{n-1} on R.R. The set of fixed points of this action is ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruled and it coincides with F​i​x​(G)Fix(G).

Hence assume that G=Ga.G=G_{a}. Let DD be the degree of ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruledness of X.X. Choose a∈F​i​x​(G).a\in Fix(G). Let ϕ:G×X∋(g,x)↦ϕ⁡(g,x)∈X\phi:G\times X\ni(g,x)\mapsto\phi(g,x)\in X be a polynomial action of GG on X.X. This action also induces a polynomial action of the complexification Gc=(ℂ,+)G^{c}=(\mathbb{C},+) of GG on XcX^{c}. We will denote this action by ϕ¯.\overline{\phi}. Assume that degg⁡ϕ≤d.\deg_{g}\phi\leq d. By Definition 4.2 it is enough to prove that there exists a polynomially parametric curve S⊂F​i​x​(G)S\subset Fix(G) passing through aa of degree bounded by d​DdD. Let LL be a polynomially parametric curve in XX passing through a.a. If it is contained in F​i​x​(G)Fix(G), then the assertion is true. Otherwise consider a closed semialgebraic surface Y=L×G.Y=L\times G. There is a natural G−G-action on YY: for h∈Gh\in G and y=(l,g)∈Yy=(l,g)\in Y we set h⁡(y)=(l,h​g)∈Y.h(y)=(l,hg)\in Y. Consider the map

Φ:L×G∋(x,g)→ϕ⁡(g,x)∈X.\Phi:L\times G\ni(x,g)\rightarrow\phi(g,x)\in X.

It is a generically finite polynomial map. Observe that it is GG-invariant, which means Φ⁡(g​y)=g​Φ​(y).\Phi(gy)=g\Phi(y). This implies that the set SΦS_{\Phi} of points at which Φ\Phi is not finite is GG-invariant. Indeed, it is enough to show that the complement of this set is GG-invariant. Let Φ\Phi be finite at x∈X.x\in X. Then there is an open neighborhood UU of xx such that Φ:Φ−1​(U)→U\Phi:\Phi^{-1}(U)\rightarrow U is finite. Now we have the following diagram:

This shows that if Φ\Phi is finite over UU, then it is finite over g​U.gU. In particular this implies that the set SΦS_{\Phi} is GG-invariant. Let SΦ=S1∪…∪SkS_{\Phi}=S_{1}\cup...\cup S_{k} be a decomposition of SΦS_{\Phi} into polynomially parametric curves (see Corollary 4.6). Since SΦS_{\Phi} is GG-invariant, each curve SiS_{i} is also GG-invariant. Note that the point aa belongs to SΦS_{\Phi}, because the fiber over aa has infinitely many points. We can assume that a∈S1.a\in S_{1}. Let us note that aa is also a fixed point for Gc.G^{c}. Let x∈S1;x\in S_{1}; we want to show that x∈F​i​x​(G).x\in Fix(G). Indeed, the set S1cS_{1}^{c} is also Gc−G^{c}-invariant and if x∉F​i​x​(G)x\not\in Fix(G) then Gc.x=S1cG^{c}.x=S_{1}^{c} and aa would be in the orbit of xx, which is a contradiction. Corollary 5.2.

Let GG be a real, non-trivial, connected, unipotent group which acts effectively and polynomially on a closed algebraic set X⊂ℝnX\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}. If the set F​i​x​(G)Fix(G) of fixed points of this action, is nowhere dense in XX, then it is ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruled.

Corollary 5.3.

Let GG be a real, non-trivial, connected, unipotent group which acts effectively and polynomially on a connected smooth closed algebraic variety X⊂ℝnX\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then the set F​i​x​(G)Fix(G) is ℝ\mathbb{R}-uniruled.
